blocks.raw:
<LawCallout code="irr" section="RA 9266, Section 27">
A person who is not a citizen of the Philippines at the time of applying to take the licensure examination shall not be allowed to take the exam unless proof exists that the foreign country either (a) admits Filipino citizens to practice architecture without restriction, or (b) allows them to practice after an examination on terms of strict and absolute equality with its own citizens, including unconditional recognition of prerequisite degrees from Philippine institutions.
</LawCallout>

blocks.raw: <Warn>The previous version of this article claimed a foreign applicant could prove "reciprocity OR substantial equivalence in education, training, and experience." This is incorrect. The phrase "substantial equivalence" does NOT appear in RA 9266 Section 27. The only pathway under the law is **proof of reciprocal treatment** by the foreign country.</Warn>

blocks.raw: <Note>**Why "law, not practice" matters.** If a foreign country merely tolerates Filipino architects working there without a written statutory right, that does not satisfy Section 27. The applicant must point to a specific legal provision in the foreign jurisdiction that grants Filipino architects equal access. This is a common exam trap: an answer choice describing a country's "established practice" of admitting Filipino architects sounds correct but fails because the law does not explicitly provide for reciprocity.</Note>

blocks.raw: <Tip>Think of these as two different doors: Section 27 leads to **full Philippine licensure** (you pass the exam, you become a licensed Philippine architect). Section 38 leads to a **temporary permit** for a specific project (you remain licensed in your home country, you work on one project with a Filipino counterpart). You go through one door or the other — not both.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <Tip>**Exam shortcut.** When reading a fact pattern about a foreign architect in the Philippines, ask: *\"Are they taking the Philippine exam?\"* If yes → Section 27 (reciprocity needed, leads to full license). If no → Section 38 (temporary permit, Filipino counterpart required, Board approval). This single question resolves most pathway-distinction items on the LEA.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <Warn>The article previously claimed the Board "maintains a list of countries with which reciprocity exists." The Board evaluates reciprocity evidence on a case-by-case or ad hoc basis. There is no widely published standing list comparable to those in other professions. The phrasing "the Board maintains a list" overstates the formalization of this process.</Warn>

blocks.raw: <ExamTip>**Exam strategy.** Reciprocity questions on the LEA usually follow one pattern: a fact scenario describing a foreign architect's situation, then a question about what they need or which section applies. The distractors often mix up Section 27 and Section 38 requirements. Write a quick 2-column table on scratch paper before reading the answer choices — one column for Section 27 (full license via exam, needs reciprocity proof, no counterpart required after passing) and one for Section 38 (temporary permit, project-specific, Filipino counterpart needed, Board approval). Then map the facts to the correct column.</ExamTip>

</AlertBox>
